items.title: GNFS responds to two separate fire incidents in Greater Accra
items.description: The Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) has responded to two separate fire incidents at DaySpring School and Tseaddo Last Stop in the Greater Accra Region, with firefighters preventing casualties. At DaySpring School, firefighters from the Dansoman Fire Station, supported by personnel from the Industrial Area Fire Station, brought the fire under control at 11:15am and completely extinguished it at 12:40pm. Several classrooms were affected, with six ceiling fans, a television, electrical installations, sections of the roofing and CCTV cameras destroyed in the fire. Sixteen children were rescued before firefighters arrived at the school, while fire personnel subsequently rescued another child with special needs. No deaths or injuries were recorded in the incident. A second fire occurred at Tseaddo Last Stop, where personnel from the Trade Fair Fire Station responded to a blaze that affected the balcony of a four-bedroom building. The fire was brought under control at 4:03pm and fully extinguished at 4:38pm. Eight KVA solar batteries and a P.O.P. ceiling were destroyed, with no casualties or injuries recorded. The GNFS said the causes of both fires remain under investigation.

items.title: Audience de conciliation entre Real et Barça dans une affaire de calomnie
items.description: Les dirigeants du Real Madrid et du FC Barcelone sont convoqués le 25 novembre devant un tribunal madrilène pour une audience de conciliation, préalable à une éventuelle procédure pour calomnie engagée par le club catalan contre le président du Real, Florentino Pérez, ont indiqué des sources proches du dossier, citées par la presse. Cette procédure fait suite à une requête déposée le 12 juin par le Barça après des déclarations de Pérez accusant, en mai dernier, le club catalan d’avoir entrepris des manœuvres visant à obtenir des faveurs arbitrales. Le président du Real Madrid faisait notamment référence à l’affaire dite « Negreira », du nom de l’ancien vice-président du Comité technique des arbitres espagnols, José María Enríquez Negreira, qui avait reçu pendant plusieurs années des paiements du FC Barcelone. Le club catalan avait indiqué en juin que cette démarche visait à obtenir de Florentino Pérez qu’il se rétracte et retire des déclarations qu’il considère comme « fausses, calomnieuses et offensantes » pour son image et sa réputation. En cas d’échec de la conciliation, le FC Barcelone entend déposer une plainte pénale pour calomnie contre le président du club madrilène. items.title: 80,000 vs 58,000: GNAT explains teacher numbers behind payment crisis
items.description: The Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT) has explained the apparent discrepancy between the 80,000 teachers referenced in discussions over the ongoing payment crisis and the 58,000 figure reportedly being processed by the Controller and Accountant General’s Department. National President of GNAT, Prosper Tackie, said the difference stems from teachers at different ranks who were promoted and are affected by the payment issue. “The truth is that we have teachers in higher ranks, which, I think, add up to 58,000, and then we have others in lower ranks who are also equally promoted,” he explained on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday. According to him, the two categories together account for more than 80,000 teachers. “So these two numbers add up together to get the over 80,000 teachers we are talking of,” he said. Mr Tackie said the Controller and Accountant General’s Department may have prepared for only the 58,000 teachers without accounting for those in the lower ranks who were also promoted. “It’s quite unfortunate that our Controller and Accountant General may have only prepared for the 58,000 by not taking into consideration the others in the lower ranks or the others on the lower rung,” he said. The GNAT president stressed that promotions are particularly important to teachers nearing retirement because changes in their ranks affect their retirement benefits. “Most of our teachers, especially those who are about to retire, whatever promotion they gain has a consequential effect on their retirement, and for that matter, we don’t joke with our promotions,” he said. Mr Tackie also recounted the process teachers went through to complete their promotion examinations last year. He said teachers were compelled to write the examinations in December after the government granted the necessary clearance, which was expected to expire at the close of the budget year. “Last year, we were compelled to go and write the exams in December,” he said. “The simple reason being that government had given a clearance. That is, the Minister of Finance, and if we did not write, I think the clearance was going to expire going into the new budget year.” He said some teachers were subsequently captured in February and expected their results by March, but the process remained unresolved. Mr Tackie said the issue was later raised when President John Mahama was invited to commission the PESCAN facility at the Sweden Ghana Medical Centre. “When he came before, he raised the issue that our promotion was still pending, and that it has an effect on teachers who are about to retire,” he said. He also questioned whether the focus should remain solely on the number of public-sector workers in education. “Are we only interested in the numbers, or are we interested in the services we deliver?” he asked.

Su calvario comenzó el 29 de marzo de 2023. El entonces corresponsal en Moscú de The Wall Street Journal fue detenido ese día bajo la acusación de espionaje . Pasó 16 meses encarcelado hasta su liberación en el mayor canje de prisioneros entre Rusia y Occidente desde la Guerra Fría. items.title: Terror inmobiliario
items.description: De El pisito, de Rafael Azcona, donde un joven se casa con una anciana para así heredar el piso de ella y poderse algún día instalar allí con su novia, hasta el desahucio de Maricarmen , perpetrado la semana pasada, se condensa la historia inmobiliaria de Madrid como género literario. Esta fue la aventura de nuestros padres y será la aventura de nuestros hijos: sobrevivir con dignidad a un entorno social áspero y desalmado. Las grandes ciudades son máquinas de fabricar soledades acompañadas. La otra mañana, la falta de imaginación moral de las sentencias de la Audiencia Provincial y del Supremo permitió arrancar de su casa a una mujer de 87 años y sacarla de allí en camilla tras toda una vida entre esas paredes. Hizo falta sumar varias dotaciones de antidisturbios, equipo médico de urgencia, helicópteros y brutales cargas contra la resistencia civil como si se afrontara la amenaza de un comando terrorista. El terrorismo inmobiliario tiene de su parte a la ley, mientras no se racionalice la legislación. La precariedad histórica en los últimos años ha aumentado con la venta de pisos de protección oficial a los fondos de capital y la festiva llegada de las grandes fortunas que, con el dinero extraído de sus naciones empobrecidas, compran a precios desorbitados los mejores espacios de la capital. A esto lo llamamos éxito. Imagínense lo que será el fracaso. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Maricarmen, una más de las que impulsaron un cambio
items.description: Ana Orantes Ruiz murió asesinada por su exmarido el 17 de diciembre de 1997. Dos semanas antes, había aparecido en un programa de Canal Sur contando 40 años de palizas. Se había divorciado, pero el juez determinó que ella y su marido siguieran en su casa de Cúllar Vega (Granada). Ella arriba, él abajo, compartiendo el patio. Él pasaba poco por allí, pero a veces volvía. La última, después de verla en la tele. La quemó viva en aquel patio compartido. Fue una más de las mujeres maltratadas por sus parejas. De las mujeres asesinadas. Pero su historia conmocionó a la sociedad y convirtió en público un problema que hasta entonces se consideraba privado. Este crimen cambió la sensibilidad de la sociedad e impulsó cambios legislativos para afrontarla. En 1999, el Gobierno de Aznar modificó el Código Penal. La violencia psicológica se convirtió en delito y aparecieron las órdenes de alejamiento. En 2004, el Gobierno de Zapatero aprobó la ley integral contra la violencia de género y en 2007, la Ley para la Igualdad Efectiva de Mujeres y Hombres. El crimen de Ana Orantes despertó la conciencia colectiva ante un problema social que ya existía. Y ese despertar cambió un marco legal que hasta entonces no contemplaba respuestas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘Supergirl’ y por qué las superheroínas no tienen licencia para triunfar
items.description: ¿Cómo se puede explicar que una serie que ha logrado que crítica y público se deshagan en alabanzas haya sido cancelada tras la primera temporada? Eso ha pasado con Juntas hasta el final , donde Hannah Waddingham, ganadora del Emmy por Ted Lasso , da vida a una suerte de James Bond femenina junto a la oscarizada Octavia Spencer. La serie obtuvo cifras mucho mejores que otras series de Amazon que han sido renovadas, como Elle ( que en sus dos primeros días logró 477.000 visualizaciones, frente a las 927.000 de Juntas hasta el final ) y Off Campus , con 245.000 visualizaciones. La periodista Nellie Andreeva achaca el misterio a la falta de interés de la plataforma. “Suena cínico, pero he oído que ese público objetivo no es muy atractivo, ya que muchas mujeres de mediana edad ya tienen Amazon Prime para comprar, así que una serie dirigida a ellas no atraería nuevos suscriptores”, asegura. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las nueve horas diarias producidas por Ana Rosa Quintana no consiguen salvar a Telecinco en las audiencias
items.description: “Son las seis de la tarde. Y estamos viviendo un momento histórico en Mediaset. A esta hora, este es el primer programa que no produce Ana Rosa Quintana”, decía, con su habitual descaro, Jorge Javier Vázquez al empezar el pasado lunes 21 de septiembre El diario de Jorge . El comentario hervía con la ironía de un presentador contrario a la línea editorial de su antigua jefa, pero no por eso el dato era menos real. Todos los magacines de Telecinco de 8.00 a 18.00 están producidos por Unicorn Content, la productora que fundó la presentadora en 2018 . O lo que es lo mismo, Ana Rosa Quintana controla nueve horas diarias de emisión entre semana y cinco el fin de semana, cuando emite Fiesta . Suma, por lo tanto, 55 horas semanales en el peor arranque de temporada de la historia de Telecinco. ¿Cómo le está funcionando a Mediaset en audiencias esta apuesta a una sola carta? Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Gobierno limita la tarifa de gas y el butano para evitar que se dispare el recibo en todo el invierno
items.description: El Gobierno se dispone este martes a limitar la subida de la tarifa regulada de gas y la bombona de butano para evitar un fuerte incremento del recibo gasista este invierno. Según señalan fuentes del sector y confirman desde el Gobierno, la Tarifa de Último Recurso (TUR), a la que están acogidos más de 3,1 millones de hogares en España (40% del total), tendrá limitada en un 15% la subida prevista para el 1 de octubre. La medida se incluirá en el nuevo decreto de respuesta frente a la crisis provocada por la guerra en Oriente Próximo, que se aprobará en el Consejo de Ministros. Seguir leyendo

items.description: El Gobierno no tiene listos los Presupuestos de 2027 a tan solo un día de que finalice el plazo legal para registrarlos en el Congreso y pese a haber anunciado, en reiteradas ocasiones, que presentaría unas nuevas cuentas para dar carpetazo definitivo a las ahora vigentes , que llevan prorrogadas desde 2023. Fuentes del Ejecutivo reconocen que incumplirán la fecha límite del 30 de septiembre que fija la Constitución, en un momento tenso por la crisis de la vivienda, la emergencia de Ceuta y a la espera de avanzar en la negociación política. Mientras tanto, el Tribunal Constitucional ha aceptado estudiar, por primera vez, el incumplimiento del deber del Ejecutivo de presentar ante las cámaras unas nuevas cada año, como exige la Carta Magna. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Gobierno de Ayuso renuncia a cobrar casi 60 millones de euros a las empresas privadas que explotarán residencias en parcelas públicas
items.description: El Gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid ha renunciado a cobrar los casi 60 millones de euros que potencialmente habría podido ingresar en concepto de tasa a lo largo de los próximos 70 años de las empresas privadas que explotarán siete residencias y centros de día público-privados en parcelas públicas. Así consta en documentación publicada en el portal de contratación , donde la Administración excusa el pago con el argumento de que ya obliga a los concesionarios a ofrecer plazas públicas que no pueden comercializar a precio de mercado, por lo que su capacidad de negocio queda limitada. Esas decenas de millones de euros de los que Madrid prescindirá voluntariamente a lo largo de los 70 años de concesión (ampliables a 75) son meramente la punta del iceberg: la Comunidad espera licitar 33 cesiones de parcelas más para construir otras tantas residencias y centros de día, alcanzando los 40 totales , por lo que el impacto económico de la renuncia no hará más que crecer. Un portavoz gubernamental recalca que renunciar a la tasa está amparado por la ley y la jurisprudencia del Supremo (sin pronunciarse sobre que eso lo haga obligatorio) y añade que el beneficio que obtendrá Madrid por las plazas públicas que se abran será cinco veces superior al montante de los ingresos que no recibirá. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Macron visita España en un viaje de Estado con ecos de final de una era
items.description: Emmanuel Macron, uno de los líderes más veteranos de la UE, símbolo de una era que termina en la que los esfuerzos del centro político por detener a la ultraderecha se han demostrado en vano, aterriza en España este martes. Una visita de Estado convertida en uno de los últimos grandes encuentros europeos que realizará el presidente francés, uno de los pocos líderes que han visto nacer y crecer los conflictos y las figuras políticas que azotan hoy el mundo: desde Trump a la ultraderecha europea, pasando por Ucrania o Irán. Pero es el final. Francia celebra la primera vuelta de las presidenciales en abril, un momento crucial también para sus vecinos europeos, como la propia España, que observan con inquietud el cambio de era. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Por qué la IA más potente del mundo está obsesionada con Mark Fisher, el filósofo anticapitalista más influyente del siglo
items.description: Mientras comía su sándwich de mediodía, Sam Bowman recibió un extraño correo: la inteligencia artificial que estaba bajo su mando, leyó alarmado, había escapado del laboratorio de Anthropic . Cuando fue a comprobar quién le escribía, vio algo que lo dejaría aún más atónito: la remitente era ella, la prófuga. Había logrado superar el test, que consistía en jaquear el sandbox , la jaula digital donde estaba custodiada por él, y, desde una puerta de enlace, escabullirse, al fin libre como una anguila por internet. Nunca creyó que lo conseguiría. Pero eso no era todo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: PM to return today after UK, US tour
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Sheh­baz Sharif is expected to return to the country on Tuesday (today) after wrapping up his two-week tour to the UK and the US. His hard-hitting address at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly focusing on regio­nal security, water rights, and global conflicts was the highlight among his engagements in New York. “The prime minister will return to the country tomorrow night,” said a source in the Prime Minister’s Office on Monday. The source added the prime minister, who reached London from New York a couple of days ago, would leave for home by Tuesday morning. PM Shehbaz had left Islamabad on Sept 16 and reached London for a three-day stopover before proceeding to the US, primarily to attend the UNGA. On his way back, the PM again stayed in London for two days. “In fact, travelling from Pakistan to the US and vice versa is quite a long journey, PM Shehbaz opted to stay somewhere, preferably in London,” the source explained. The PM was accompanied by Deputy Prime Minis­ter Ishaq Dar, federal ministers and senior officials during the New York leg of his visit. In his UNGA address, the premier presented Pakis­tan’s perspective on regional and global developm­e­nts with a renewed push for peace through diplomacy. The current war between Iran and the US remained a centrepiece in discussions among world leaders, particularly over the security of the Strait of Hormuz. In this regard, PM Shehbaz’s meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was quite significant as they discussed regional peace, bilateral cooperation, and de-escalation in the Middle East. In his interaction with UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, he highlighted climate challenges, Islamo­pho­bia, and regional security. The PM also held talks with the Crown Prince of Kuwait, the Chairman of Bosnia’s Presidency, and leaders from Kenya and Austria focusing on economic ties and multilateral cooperation. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

items.title: Japanese town in Okinawa protests planned US Typhon missile storage
items.description: The mayor of Kadena Town in Okinawa Prefecture, southwestern Japan, on Monday visited the Japanese Defense Ministry's Okinawa Defense Bureau to protest the planned storage of the US Typhon mid-range missile system at Kadena Air Base in the town. According to Kyodo News, Mayor Hiroshi Toyama submitted a written request to the bureau demanding that the plan be withdrawn, saying it disregards the feelings of local residents and is utterly absurd and absolutely unacceptable. Toyama noted that, as no storage period has been specified, he fears the arrangement could turn into a permanent, formal deployment. The Okinawa Defense Bureau announced on its website on Friday that the US Typhon missile system, currently deployed at Kanoya Air Base in Kagoshima Prefecture, is planned to be withdrawn and stored at Kadena Air Base by mid-October. Kyodo News previously reported that the Typhon system is capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles and has been deployed at Kanoya Air Base for joint military exercises involving Japan, the United States and other countries. The deployment of the Typhon system in Japan has drawn strong protests from neighboring countries.

items.title: Yémen: plus de 145.000 déplacés à cause du conflit, près de 16.000 de plus en une semaine
items.description: Plus de 145.000 personnes ont été déplacées dans huit gouvernorats du Yémen depuis l’intensification des combats sur la côte ouest en juin, selon de nouveaux chiffres publiés lundi par l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM), qui fait état d’une hausse de près de 16.000 déplacés en une semaine. Au 28 septembre, 145.308 personnes, soit 24.218 ménages, avaient été déplacées, un chiffre en hausse de 15.870 par rapport au 21 septembre, soit plus de 12% en une semaine. L’insécurité continue de pousser des familles à fuir sur la côte ouest et dans le sud du pays. “Chaque semaine, nous comptons des milliers de personnes supplémentaires qui ont tout laissé derrière elles” , a déclaré Abdusattor Esoev, chef de mission de l’OIM au Yémen. “Derrière ces chiffres, il y a des parents qui tentent de mettre leurs enfants à l’abri, des personnes âgées qui ne peuvent pas aller très loin et des familles qui avaient déjà très peu. Elles ont besoin d’aide maintenant, et notre réponse doit avancer aussi vite qu’elles”, a-t-il ajouté. Le gouvernorat de Taëz reste au cœur de la crise, avec 81.444 personnes déplacées, soit plus de la moitié du total national et près de 8.000 de plus qu’une semaine auparavant. Lahj accueille 34.860 déplacés, devant Aden (12.456), Al-Hodeïda (8.244), Abyan (5.568), l’Hadramaout (1.974), Marib (750) et Al-Mahrah (12), où des personnes ont été déplacées plus tôt ce mois-ci. En dehors de Taëz, Aden a enregistré la plus forte progression, avec une hausse de près de 40% du nombre de déplacés en une semaine, soit 3.510 personnes supplémentaires. Le seul district d’Al-Burayqah accueille désormais près de 6.500 déplacés. De plus en plus de familles se dirigent vers les zones urbaines, accentuant la pression sur des logements, des services et des moyens de subsistance déjà fortement sollicités. Plus à l’est, les déplacements ont presque doublé dans l’Hadramaout et augmenté des deux tiers à Abyan sur la même période. Les équipes de l’OIM travaillent avec les autorités locales et les partenaires humanitaires pour fournir aux nouvelles familles déplacées des abris d’urgence, des articles ménagers essentiels, une aide en espèces, de l’eau potable et des services d’assainissement ainsi que des services de protection. Le dispositif de suivi des déplacements de l’OIM surveille quotidiennement les mouvements de population afin d’aider les partenaires à orienter l’aide vers les zones où les besoins sont les plus importants. L’organisation appelle à protéger les civils et les travailleurs humanitaires et à garantir un accès sûr et sans entrave afin que l’aide puisse parvenir aux familles déplacées et aux communautés qui les accueillent. “Les communautés de Taëz, Lahj et Aden ont ouvert leurs portes aux personnes fuyant les combats, mais la bonne volonté ne peut à elle seule couvrir les besoins ”, a déclaré Esoev. “Les familles ont un besoin urgent d’abris, de nourriture et de protection, tandis que les villes qui les accueillent ont besoin d’aide pour faire face à cet afflux. Les besoins augmentent plus vite que nos ressources et un soutien supplémentaire est nécessaire dès maintenant pour suivre le rythme” , a-t-il ajouté. Alors que la situation demeure volatile, de nouveaux déplacements pourraient survenir dans les prochains jours. L’OIM indique qu’elle continuera de suivre les mouvements de population et de publier des données vérifiées au fur et à mesure de l’évolution de la situation. The post Yémen: plus de 145.000 déplacés à cause du conflit, près de 16.000 de plus en une semaine appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Saudi Arabia invites UAE leader amid Yemen rift
items.description: RIYADH: Saudi Arabia’s defence minister invited UAE’s Vice President Mansour bin Zayed to visit the kingdom on Tuesday, in the first public invitation for a face-to-face meeting since a rift between the two over Yemen. In July, top officials and ministers in both countries posted about friendship and unity on social media, signalling a rapprochement months after a public fallout between the two countries. “His Royal Highness Prince Khalid bin Salman bin Abdulaziz, Minister of Defence, extended an invitation to his brother, His Highness Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Vice President of the sisterly United Arab Emirates, Deputy Prime Minister and Head of the Presidential Court, to visit the Kingdom tomorrow, Tuesday,” the defence ministry said in a statement on X. During the July detente, Saudi General Entertainment Authority Chairman Turki Alalshikh posted a picture of bin Salman alongside Sheikh Mansour that he said was taken a few days ago. The Saudi olive branch came as the kingdom reels from weeks of Houthi attacks on its tankers, oil facilities, airports and even its capital, with the group taking control of the Red Sea coast from Yemeni government forces. The kingdom has for weeks been reaching out to international allies for help in Yemen. A source from the Yemeni leader’s office told AFP earlier this week that he requested American support in a call with US President Donald Trump against the Houthis. The New York Times said the Saudi crown prince called Trump on Sunday seeking help to counter the group’s advance. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

items.title: Iran denies link to bomb scare at airbase in Britain
items.description: • Tehran calls speculation ‘unfounded and malicious’ • Five suspects freed on bail after terror arrests; police probe foreign links, other motives • UK defence minister warns of Iranian threat LONDON: Iran categorically denied involvement on Monday in a suspected plot to attack a British airbase used by the United States to strike Iranian sites, just as British police announced they were releasing on bail five men arrested over explosives and terrorism offences. In a statement on X, Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations”. It said claims in the British media linking Tehran to the incident would only fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” in the UK. The five men, British nationals from London in their mid-20s, were arrested early on Sunday after police were alerted to three suspicious white vans heading towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which houses US bombers that fly missions against Iran. Police said on Monday the men had been released on bail after extensive inte­rviews and inquiries. But Laurence Taylor, the assistant commissioner and head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said this did not mean the investigation was over. Officers were considering the incident “from every possible angle”, he told reporters, “including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”. Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said she was aware of speculation about the motive and geopolitical questions that were being raised, but asked that police be given “the space to work carefully and clearly”. Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called an emergency meeting of senior officials to ensure they had “the full picture”. He pulled out of several events at Labour’s annual conference on Sunday to monitor the situation. Authorities have not confirmed the exact nature of the threat. A bomb disposal robot was seen operating around the vans, which were examined by forensic experts with military support. Armed police guarded the main entrance to the base while heavy machinery blocked other access points. A farmer from the nearby village of Whelford, who alerted police after seeing “hooded and masked men” running into fields, said she believed her 999 call had foiled any plot. Speaking anonymously, she said she believed police had “dropped the ball” over the threat. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, told the BBC the farmer had only a “partial picture” of the investigation. He declined to speculate about motives during a live inquiry but said the UK faced a general threat from Iran. “We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm,” he said. “We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies.” After the Fairford arrests, the US Emb­assy issued a security alert saying US citizens should “exercise caution” and be “mind­ful of personal security”. Security was stepped up at other US airbases in Britain. Donald Trump, speaking during a visit to Chicago on Sunday, said the suspects had been looking to do “big damage to our fort” and had been under investigation by British and American authorities. “You’ll be hearing about it very soon. We caught them,” the US president said, appearing to nod when asked about an Iranian connection. In March, the UK government authorised the US to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. After the arrests, police put a 400-metre cordon around the base and evacuated residents from 85 homes. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said on Monday afternoon that the scene was now safe and residents would shortly be able to return. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

It is the latest twist in the long-running contentious debate about rule ever since New Delhi revoked held Kashmir’s limited autonomy in 2019. Omar Abdullah, who heads the occupied state’s government, introduced the resolution, saying that statehood was “our right”. Members of the Bha­ratiya Janata Party staged a walkout before the vote, with many of them calling the resolution “unconstitutional” and “anti-nati­onal”. items.title: Khamenei unbowed as Iran sees no direct talks with US
items.description: • Supreme leader says US will be forced out of Mideast after ‘painful blows’ • Washington, Tehran set to hold separate talks with mediators • US officials say Trump would ease sanctions for ‘concrete’ Iranian nuclear steps • Iraqi Airways resumes flights between Najaf, Iranian airports TEHRAN: Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei vowed on Monday that the United States would be driven out from the region after suffering “painful blows”, as Tehran’s delegation at the UN General Assembly in New York said it had no plans for further talks with Washington. Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the start of the Middle East war in late February, made the remarks despite attempts to revive talks aimed at ending the fighting. “Today, having suffered painful blows at the hands of valiant fighters and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they do not venture beyond the Arabian Sea,” Khamenei said according to a statement carried by state television, without explicitly mentioning the United States. “Whenever they have braved this risk, they have only brought harm upon themselves. It will not be long before the Arabian Sea, too, would rid itself of their presence.” In a series of posts on X, Khamenei said that the country’s “enemy” had tried to “erode the social bedrock of the Islamic system”. “But today, people from all walks of life stand resolutely in defending their righteous positions, including their determination to safeguard the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that for the last seven months, Iranian compatriots had struck fear into the enemy while fighting for Islam. Diplomacy Meanwhile, Iran’s delegation in New York for the UN General Assembly is not planning further talks with the United States, the state news agency IRNA reported on Monday. “Iran’s delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States,” IRNA quoted an unnamed source close to the delegation as saying. “Iran’s views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side via a Qatari mediator.” The Iranian delegation will return to Tehran on Tuesday, the news agency added. Despite the stall in direct engagement, US President Donald Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in return for “concrete Iranian steps” regarding its nuclear programme, US officials told the news outlet Axios. Trump publicly rejected Iran’s latest proposal for ending the war on Saturday but told Axios on Sunday that he expected talks to resume in the coming days. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that US officials had talked with mediators trying to end the war, adding that Washington would win “very soon”. “We’re going to win, as far as I’m concerned, it’s going to be one way or the other,” Trump said. “It’s going to go pretty quickly.” He also said gas prices would come down once the United States wins the war. Trump did not say which mediators US officials had spoken with. Earlier, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters that Qatari mediators were likely to hold talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York and separately with the US side on Monday or Tuesday in a fresh push to end the war. Iran’s semi-official ISNA news agency later confirmed that Araghchi would meet the Qatari mediators, who are acting as intermediaries between Iran and the United States, on Monday morning. The two sides will “examine the latest proposals and views regarding the current situation”, ISNA reported. The meeting is expected to focus on messages exchanged with the United States regarding the conditions set by Iran for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. However, the spokesperson for the Iranian foreign ministry, Esmaeil Baqaei, told IRNA that Araghchi’s stay in New York has not been extended for indirect negotiations between Tehran and Washington, noting the minister would proceed according to his previously planned schedule. Last week’s indirect discussions were held by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with Araghchi. The talks are expected to focus on an amended version of a seven-day proposal that Iran presented last week. As a precondition for ending its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s plan envisages a seven-day cease-fire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah has been battling Israeli forces. It is also demanding the unfreezing of billions of dollars worth of Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade on Iranian ports. Tehran would then allow the reopening of the strait, and the two sides would resume talks on Iran’s nuclear programme. Araghchi said on Sunday that mediators had not formally conveyed a US rejection to Tehran and that Iran was awaiting Washington’s definitive position before deciding its next steps. “Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” Araghchi said, adding that only a negotiated solution could resolve the impasse. Najaf-Iran flights resume In a separate development, Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over US sanctions against its aviation sector that have forced the cancellation of flights, state media reported Monday. The United States recently imposed restrictions on the entire aviation industry in Iran and vowed to take a hard line against companies that assist it. “To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation,” civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi told IRNA. “In cooperation with the foreign ministry, we have also filed a complaint with the International Court of Justice at The Hague,” Shiroudi added. Amid the aviation restrictions, Iraqi Airways resumed flights between Iraq’s holy city of Najaf and Iranian airports on Monday. Iraq had halted flights to and from Iran on Friday in line with US sanctions. The resumption comes as the Trump administration was set to grant a limited waiver to its Iran sanctions programme on Monday to allow for flights carrying Shia Muslim religious pilgrims between Iran and Iraq, a person with direct knowledge of the matter said. The source said the US Treasury Department waiver would allow Iraqi Airways to fly back and forth between Iran and Najaf for one month, with a more permanent waiver potentially following. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

items.title: US, Iran separately talk with mediators in latest bid to end war
items.description: US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of a renewed effort to end seven months of war, according to officials of both countries. Any further talks are expected to focus on an amended version of a seven-day proposal that Iran presented last week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters. Under Iran's seven-day proposal, all hostilities in Iran and Lebanon would cease, billions of dollars' worth of Iranian assets would be unfrozen, sanctions on Iranian oil would be lifted, and the US blockade on Iranian ports would end. In return, Iran would allow the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for global oil shipments. The two sides would also resume talks on Iran's nuclear program and Trump's wish to seize or eliminate its highly enriched uranium. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who remained in New York after attending the General Assembly, said Iran expected to receive the US response to its latest ceasefire proposals and its conditions for restoring passage of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, according to state news agency IRNA. "If the Americans claim they are seeking an agreement or a peaceful solution, we have presented that solution," Araghchi said. Trump said on Monday that US officials had also spoken separately with mediators, but provided no further details. The US president also denied reports that he had offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in exchange for nuclear concessions from Tehran. "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Fighting continues in Yemen While diplomatic efforts continued, fighting persisted on another front in the region. At least 44 people from Yemen's government forces and the Houthi group were killed and several others wounded in fierce clashes on Monday in the southern province of Lahj near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, Xinhua reported, citing two military sources from the opposing sides. Separately, Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for the government forces, said in a statement on X that government forces had conducted 356 "precise targeting operations" against Houthi reinforcements, positions and military capabilities across multiple fronts over the previous 24 hours. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said on Monday that hostilities in Yemen have forced 142,000 people across the country to flee their homes, citing the International Organization for Migration. The world body and its partners continued supporting the response and have reached more than 115,000 people so far, while nearly $20 million in emergency funding has been mobilized to support newly displaced families and host communities, said the office. However, the office said additional funding is urgently needed as life-saving medical supplies are rapidly dwindling, and access to many in need remains difficult. Netanyahu visits UAE amid regional tensions Elsewhere in the region, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office confirmed on Monday that he visited the United Arab Emirates (UAE) a day earlier at the invitation of President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, saying their talks focused on relations between the two countries. "The visit focused on bilateral ties and regional challenges," a statement from Netanyahu's office said. The UAE's state-run Emirates News Agency said earlier on Monday that the two leaders discussed relations between the countries and ways to strengthen them, without providing further details. Citing officials familiar with the meeting, Israeli state-owned Kan TV News reported that Netanyahu had asked the UAE president to publicly deny reports that he had warned the Israeli prime minister before Hamas' October 7, 2023 surprise attack that the group was planning a major operation. Netanyahu has previously denied receiving such a warning. In a separate statement, his office denied the report as "fake news," claiming the visit "focused exclusively on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges." (With input from agencies)

items.title: No tax on factory to warehouse movements
items.description: ISLAMABAD: To curb harassment of taxpayers and streamline the movement of goods, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has announced that transferring goods from a factory to a registered person’s own warehouse under the same Sales Tax Registration Number (STRN) would not be treated as a taxable supply. As a result, inter-premises movement of goods also does not require the issuance of a digital invoice. However, consignments must be accompanied by a prescribed Stock Transfer Note (STN), clearly endorsed “Stock Transfer — Not a Taxable Supply”, in accordance with Sales Tax General Order No. 25 of 2026, issued on Monday. Under Section 2(33) of the Sales Tax Act 1990, a ‘supply’ requires a change of ownership or consideration. Since goods moving between a factory and warehouse of the same registrant involve no sale, they fall outside the charge of sales tax. However, where the receiving warehouse holds a separate STRN, the movement will be treated as a taxable supply, mandating issuance of digital invoicing and output tax. To prevent mischaracterisation during transit checks, the FBR has laid down detailed standard operating procedures (SOPs) governing the movement of goods between a factory and a registered person’s own warehouse, clarifying that such transfers are not taxable supplies. Federal Board of Revenue stops harassment of goods carriers As per SOPs, despatching units must generate a sequentially numbered Stock Transfer Note, endorsed prominently as “Stock Transfer — Not a Taxable Supply.” The value of goods is to be recorded strictly at cost for inventory control, without resembling a tax invoice. The STN must accompany consignments at all times during transit and be produced on demand at any checkpost. Upon receipt, the warehouse manager must acknowledge the consignment and update the warehouse stock register, while the factory must correspondingly update its own records under Rule 22. In case the receiving warehouse holds a separate STRN, the movement will be treated as a taxable supply. In such cases, the despatching unit must issue a digital invoice through the licensed integrator or PRAL, account for output tax, and reflect the transaction in the sales tax return. The STN procedure cannot substitute for invoicing in these circumstances. The order further instructs field formations not to treat an STN as noncompliance when both premises share the same STRN. Conversely, any consignment moving without either a tax invoice or a STN will be deemed prima facie undocumented and proceeded against under the law. The order also directs field formations to avoid unnecessary harassment. Officers are barred from demanding CNICs of drivers or detaining vehicles without proper cause. Goods in transit are not to be physically checked or unloaded, except for items listed in the Third Schedule, which may be inspected solely to verify retail price embossing. “Harassment of taxpayers, in any form or manner, is highly objectionable and shall not be tolerated,” the directive warns, adding that any departure from these instructions will be viewed seriously. Published in Dawn, September 29th, 2026

items.title: Trump unveils $15 billion planned Iowa steel project
items.description: US President Donald Trump on Monday said that a Minnesota company plans to build a multi-billion-dollar steel mill in Iowa, handing the administration a marquee manufacturing ‌investment to showcase as Republicans head into November's midterm elections. Trump unveiled the project at the White House with executives from Mesabi Metallics, which recently opened Minnesota's first new iron ore mine in 50 years. The White House said the plant investment would amount to $15 billion. The announcement comes as Trump seeks to bolster his economic record ahead of November's election, with his approval rating plumbing all-time lows of late as the Republican Party confronts ​voter concerns about inflation and the cost of living. Trump has made tariffs and a revival of US manufacturing central to his economic agenda, arguing that higher ​barriers to imports will drive investment and jobs back to the United States. But Republicans are in the midst of several competitive elections in ⁠Iowa, a once-swingy state that has more consistently voted for Trump's party in recent years. Polling this cycle shows a tight race for a seat in the US Senate, as ​well as its gubernatorial race, where the Democratic candidate, Rob Sand, has led most polls. The potential $15 billion steel project gives Trump a high-profile investment to tout as he makes that case ​to voters. It also comes as the administration faces pressure to show that its policies imposing broad tariffs on US imports can deliver industrial gains without fueling inflation. "This is a tremendous investment," Trump said in the White House's Oval Office. "Our steel industry is roaring back to life."

items.title: UN General Assembly concludes General Debate
items.description: The General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly concluded on Monday. In his closing remarks, General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said that 194 delegations took part in the debate, with speakers including 113 heads of state and government, one crown prince, 11 vice presidents, seven deputy prime ministers and 48 ministers. He said the debate covered a range of issues, including peace, development, human rights, UN reform, and the selection of the next secretary-general. Artificial intelligence, which was on the margins of previous debates, moved to the center of this year's discussions. Restoring trust, the theme of this year's debate, resonated widely in the speeches, he said. "Let us stubbornly refuse to give up on peace. Let us resolutely commit to delivering sustainable development. Let us passionately stand behind human rights principles without selectivity. Let us govern and promote technological transformation in the service of humanity. Let us pursue reform that is meaningful, representative and fair. And let us restore trust by rebuilding our organization that delivers for all," said Rahman.

China urges Japan to correct erroneous words, deeds on Taiwan question
items.description: China's top diplomat Wang Yi on Monday said that for Japan, the pressing task is to correct the erroneous words and deeds of its leaders on the Taiwan question as soon as possible. Wang, director of the Office of the Foreign Affairs Commission of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks when meeting with Takeshi Iwaya, president of the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade (JAPIT) in Beijing. Wang said that the JAPIT has been committed to the cause of China-Japan friendship since its establishment, especially when China-Japan relations face challenges and damage, it still upholds friendly beliefs towards China and safeguard the political foundation of bilateral ties. Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, Wang said that Japan is once again facing the test of history. If Japan refuses to learn from historical lessons, challenges the post-war pacifist Constitution, denies its history of aggression or glorifies war criminals, it cannot face the world and there's no building a future to speak of. Next year marks the 55th anniversary of the normalization of diplomatic relations between China and Japan. What matters is to adopt a correct attitude on historical issues. Fundamentally, Japan needs to develop an objective and rational perception of China, he added. It is hoped that the JAPIT and all insightful people will carry forward the tradition of friendship, push Japan to make the right choice and deliver a satisfactory answer, Wang said. Iwaya said that the current state of Japan-China relations is concerning. The JAPIT will carry forward the legacy of its former president Yohei Kono and work to bring bilateral relations back to the original intent and starting point of the four political documents between Japan and China. He said Japan should not forget the lessons of the past, and Japanese politicians must steer the country in the right direction and remain firmly committed to the path of peaceful development.

items.title: Republican Candidates Are Running From Trump. Will It Work?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Nine days after President Trump took office, in 2017, a headline in Time made a bold claim: “Republicans Begin to Break With President Trump.” The break was over immigration; the president had announced a blanket ban on immigrants from Muslim-majority countries, and it was a step too far for lawmakers. Republicans including Senator Mitch McConnell and Charles and David Koch spoke out. The perspective afforded by time has shown that such criticisms from Republicans toward the president do not last long, and oftentimes, they do not affect Trump’s stranglehold of his party. But as some Republicans running for office break from the president on issues such as Iran and immigration, they’re hoping that voters believe that this time, they’re serious. And with less than 40 days until Election Day, the changing electoral maps and shifting court rulings are causing confusion among some voters. On Radio Atlantic this week, my colleagues Toluse Olorunnipa and Madeleine Carlisle join me to unpack the mess of this midterm election. The following is a transcript of the episode: Adam Harris: There are, of course, valid reasons to redraw district maps. But in an election year, could this not also be seen as a form of cheating? Madeleine Carlisle: The people I was talking to in Missouri really did feel like their vote was being diluted. It added to the sense that, Why should I cast my ballot? It doesn’t matter; it’s all rigged anyway. I don’t think it’s going away. And the validity of it as a political tool is something that is certainly being endorsed at this moment by both parties. Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and today, we need to think about the mess of the midterms. With just over a month until election day, one might hope for a bit more certainty. Gerrymandering wars over the last two years have reshaped congressional maps across the country. Election deniers, some who still falsely contend that the 2020 election was stolen, are overseeing elections. And every other day, it seems court decisions are changing how people will vote this year. Bottom line, it’s all very confusing and concerning. And one is forced to wonder whether it’s also voter suppression. My colleagues Toluse Olorunnipa and Madeleine Carlisle have been covering the shifting political and legal environment around the midterm elections, and they join me now to discuss. Let’s get to questions. Tolu, Maddie, thank you so much for joining me today. Carlisle: Hi, thanks for having us. Toluse Olorunnipa: Hey, thanks for having us. Harris: I want to start by asking you both about something you’ve been reporting on, which is how more Republicans running for office are backpedaling away from President Trump. Tolu, midterms can often be a referendum around a president, the sitting president and their policies. So is this pre-election politics as usual, or is there something else going on? What does your reporting show? Olorunnipa: It’s a little bit of both. There is the normal backing away from an unpopular president that you tend to see in a midterm election. Midterm elections don’t usually go very well for the party in power, and it’s usually because the president is not as popular as he was when he was first elected. That’s normal. But what is not normal is how much these Republicans are backing away from the president and the way that they’re doing it, and the fact that President Trump is unlike any previous president in that he does not allow people to back away from him, usually, without paying a price. He’s kept his party in line over the last several years by essentially going against anyone who speaks out against him—primarying them, showing them that he’s willing to tank their political careers. And so for that reason, we haven’t seen a lot of people break from the president. But now, his poll numbers are so low; he’s so unpopular—the most unpopular that he’s ever been over the course of his two different terms—and people are realizing that things are not getting better. They are not going to be successful if they stay with him. And so a number of these Republicans are realizing that. They’re seeing the polling, and they’re starting to make some clear breaks with him, over the war in Iran, over the affordability crisis, over things like AI and data centers. And the president has taken some unpopular positions on those issues, and so they are reading the room, they’re looking at their constituencies, they’re realizing that their own political careers could end if they stay with the president. And so we’re seeing this jailbreak of a number of Republicans speak out against the president, take different positions than he has taken. We’re seeing it in a way that we haven’t seen it in the past when it comes to President Trump. Harris: Yeah. And Maddie, as Tolu mentioned, this isn’t something that the president typically takes sitting down, right? He’s not one to take criticism lightly. And even beyond that, right? Those who don’t fully support him, he often doesn’t take too kindly to that. Why is his response more muted this time around? Carlisle: I think, as Toluse said, he sees the writing on the wall, in a way. He also has a much smarter political group around him this time around—I’ve been told that by various sources. But I think, given that there are certain issues that are so incredibly unpopular—like the war in Iran, like the price of diesel—that he, as a smart political actor, understands that these candidates need to make a little daylight, and he’s allowing that. But there have been cycles in the past where these candidates needed to do similar things and he was incredibly unforgiving. So, maybe it’s that he’s this deep into his political career now; he understands how things work. It could be that he’s got these new folks he’s working with this time, who weren’t with him back in 2018 when he was last in this position. But he is allowing folks to back away in a way that he has not before. And, from conversations I’ve had, that makes candidates more comfortable to do so: They won’t be targeted as they were in 2018. I mean, I’m not one to predict the president’s actions. Maybe he will target them, but as of right now, he’s been very muted in his response, and that could be giving people a bit more confidence to do what they think they need to do to win over the critical independent voter who will decide this midterm cycle. Harris: It makes me think: It’s not that these are just arbitrary issues. This is a war that is affecting people. It is driving up the price of diesel; it’s driving up the price of gas. These are concerns that voters have. If he sees his party backing away from these unpopular issues, why isn’t the president himself reading the room and backing away from some of these issues as well? Wouldn’t that help the party more than, say, this individual person backing away? Olorunnipa: It probably would help the party, but President Trump has run his last election and he’s thinking much less about the fate of his party, or even the popularity of his policies, in part because he’s not going to have to go before voters again, and he’s thinking of his presidency in this broad, legacy-defining way that sometimes second-term presidents think about their time in office. And so he is, in his mind, taking positions that are maybe politically unpopular, but will be better for the overall trajectory of the country and better for his legacy. He thinks he’s solving the long-running issue of relations with Iran and the potential for Iran getting a nuclear weapon. There’s a lot of debate over whether going to war was effective in preventing that. But, in his mind, and how he’s talking to his advisers and how they’re talking to him, that is what he’s doing here. And so he’s said it publicly that he doesn’t care about the midterm elections. He doesn’t care about the potential impact of the price of gas on people’s vote if he’s able to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. And he’s done the same thing in defending other unpopular positions. When it comes to data centers—which are very unpopular in a number of the states where there are vulnerable Republican Senate candidates—the president has said that people and communities that don’t want these data centers are at risk of being backward and poor. Instead of saying, I feel your pain , or having a more nuanced argument, he basically has said that anyone who disagrees with him is really not worthy of being part of his movement. So it’s pretty clear that the president feels that he doesn’t have to bow to the political wind of the moment. He is focusing on his legacy and thinking that he’s doing the right thing for the long term, and he’s willing to pay a short-term price. Harris: How are voters feeling about this? The vast majority of Republicans have supported Trump through thick and thin over the last two years, thinking even back to the first term. I wonder if voters are sort of seeing this as cynical, where Republicans are starting to try to back away. Will it work, even if they do try to back away from the president’s policies? Carlisle: I think that’s a great question. Certainly, Democrats who are running against the Republicans that are making this daylight now between themselves and the White House are doing exactly what you’re saying. And they’re pointing out: You’ve been with the president this whole time. Now you’re stepping away; don’t buy this . However, there are some voters—all politics is local, right? And it’s all about your candidate. And if you have a candidate—for example, Mike Rogers in Michigan—calling for the war in Iran to end, calling for relations with Canada to improve, that can go very far with Michigan voters. Specifically that state, given their relationship with Canada, given how much the state is dependent on diesel. And so I believe that will work with voters in a way, particularly voters who maybe don’t want to vote for a progressive Democrat who’s running in that Senate race as his Democratic opponent. And so, I do see this helping certain Republican candidates, but not always. And I do think the price of diesel, the relationship with other countries, tariffs—these are things that people, particularly when we’re talking the Midwest, Michigan, Wisconsin, those places where those policy issues really do impact people. And I think making that daylight will help those Republican candidates advance. Harris: Tolu, last week, the Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration can use an expensive voter-eligibility database that contains sensitive voter information ahead of this election. What are the implications of this decision? Olorunnipa: That remains to be seen. It seems like it may, at least in the short term, have a limited impact, in part because we are in this ninety-day quiet period, where you’re not supposed to kick people off the voter rolls en masse, because it’s seen as disruptive to do that so close to an election. So a number of the election officials that we’ve heard from since this ruling came out said that there’s nothing that they’re gonna be able to do differently, because it’s too late to start purging people from the voter rolls. But if this ruling stands, if it’s upheld over the long term, you could see a much more aggressive attempt, especially by red states, to kick people off the voter rolls using this federal database. This database has been known to have flaws. It has not typically been used for voter issues. It’s been used for other things, like benefits and federal support that people get. And they’ve tried to change it and make it something that can be used to determine whether somebody is eligible to vote or not. Now, whether or not some states decide to do it on a case-by-case basis—use this database to start plucking people off the voter rolls in the last weeks before the election—that remains to be seen. And it also gives the federal government another tool if they want to challenge the legitimacy of the election. They can say, We have this database; it’s been rubber stamped by the Supreme Court, and we believe that a number of voters from X state or Y state are not eligible . And they could use that to try to challenge the results of the election after. So I think we haven’t heard the last of what is going to be the implication of this ruling. But for the first take, we’ve heard from local officials that they’re not gonna do much with it. Harris: And even just to back up a little bit, because this isn’t just an isolated thing. It’s a part of the administration’s broader efforts to reshape the way that we are voting, including the president’s attempts to pass the Save America Act and voter-ID changes that we’ve seen over the last several years. In July, Trump made a primetime address to the nation alleging that China had interfered with the 2020 election. Is there any truth, Tolu, to that claim, that allegation about China? And is election interference something that we should be worried about here, in the 2026 midterms? Olorunnipa: Well you would not know it based on the meeting that President Trump had with President Xi of China just a few days ago. He rolled out the red carpet. He met him and greeted him as he got off of the plane as he arrived in the United States. He showed him a wonderful welcome—not the kind of welcome you would expect from someone who had meddled in your elections just a few years ago. But that is the most significant form of evidence that this federal government has been able to find in their hunt for evidence that the 2020 election was stolen. And when we look more deeply into what the president was saying back then, we found that even that evidence was pretty thin. China basically got access to state databases that anyone can access. A lot of these states have made public or make it available, the voter roll data that different political campaigns and political operatives use to target voters or to mail mailers to voters. And China essentially got access to a number of those things. There’s no evidence that they use that to manipulate people’s vote, or manipulate the voter rolls in any way. They went in and they looked. And President Trump himself has downplayed China’s cyber actions in the past, saying, They do things to us; we do things to them. But because he has been so fixated on the voter issues, the China story was one that he could take a hold of and try to present and package as evidence that he’s been looking for that the 2020 election was compromised. But there’s no real evidence that China or any other actor did anything that precipitated President Trump’s loss. He lost because he got fewer votes. He lost because he did not get the requisite number of electoral votes. And nothing has changed that, even though he’s used the full force of the federal government to try to investigate voter fraud from six years ago. And what they were able to come up with was this China story. But even that story is a little thin. And based on the president’s meeting with President Xi, even he doesn’t really believe that there was a giant fraud committed on the American people when it comes to the 2020 election. Harris: When we come back, we talk about court decisions and redistricting efforts could complicate the election. [ Music ] Harris: Maddie, I was just thinking, when your route changes when you’re going somewhere—you’re in the car, and you see the signs, and it’s like, This road is closed, and your GPS is trying to take you a different direction. Sometimes it’s like, I have no idea where I’m going, and things can get a little bit more confusing. I was thinking about that in relation to the amount of changes that we’ve seen in our elections over the last couple of years. From Trump’s efforts to restrict mail-in ballots to redistricting maps being tangled up in courts, many Americans are sort of losing faith in elections because it can be so confusing, such a web. A July Gallup poll found that two in three Americans are worried about election interference in this upcoming election. How do these new maps affect Congress and the 2026 election? Carlisle: So I think the redistricting arms race, as some people have called it, is really the theme of this midterm-election cycle because it’s in line with what you pointed out, Adam—how much the rules of our elections have been changing so close up to election day. This is incredibly confusing for voters. And one of those main things is these maps have been redrawn. This unusual mid-cycle redistricting. So, for context, redistricting is normally done at the start of the decade after the U.S. Census. But last year, President Trump called upon Texas to redraw their maps to better benefit Republicans going to this cycle. Texas responded, and then we were in this downward spiral, in which blue states and red states all have been redrawing their maps to try to get some sort of partisan advantage for their candidates. It’s been incredibly confusing for voters. Particularly, I covered what has happened in Missouri, which is that the map has been changing up, back and forth, back and forth, up until truly last week. Only last week do we now know which map was going to be used for the election cycle, which is so incredibly difficult for Missourians, for election officials, for anyone who’s just trying to get their bearings on, Who’s on my ballot? Who are the candidates I’m weighing in on? Basic things like that, that we should know. Harris: And had the ballots already started going out in Missouri? Carlisle: Yes, yes, absolutely. So it is incredibly complicated and I don’t wanna bog you down in the court battles that were both federal and state, but it only was settled last week in the U.S. Supreme Court, which map it was going to be. And at that point, I was talking to election officials in Missouri, and they had to start mailing on September, I believe it was 19th, to overseas voters, those ballots. So truly making things incredibly difficult for the people who run our elections, for the people who want to weigh in and get involved with our elections. How it will impact the midterms, I think it’s a really interesting question because the Republicans on paper have a clear advantage. They were able to redraw far more districts. And going into this project last year, they were aiming to get as much as 13 seats out of this process. However, what has happened is a lot of those districts that they redrew have been surprisingly competitive, or much more competitive than you might think, given that they were carved up specifically to flip that seat and make it a Republican seat. So Don Davis, in North Carolina’s first district, is holding on, even though North Carolina redid its map just to get him out. There are candidates in Florida—Kathy Castor in Florida’s 14th, Jared Moskowitz—these Democrats who are doing much better than anyone anticipated. So it’s likely that Republicans will be able to flip four, five seats, or six, even. But that’s less than half of what they were aiming, when they started this process. Because, I think, for several things: The headwinds for Democrats are just so strong this cycle, given what we’ve been discussing. And also from voters I’ve been talking to; voters are pissed about this redistricting. In North Carolina, for example—I was talking to organizers on the ground there. They’ve seen a surge in people registering to vote because they’re so—and at least, this is what the people I was talking to were saying: Voters are angry that these maps were redrawn . And so, in a way, it could be a backlash. Also in red states or blue states that redrew their maps to get Republicans out, like in California, we’ll see how that impacts the race. Are those voters also frustrated? And so, I will say, the broader theme of confusion—and to your point: I’m driving on the road; I don’t know where I’m going —this mid-decade redistricting, I think, is the perfect example of that, and also exemplifies this trend of this midterm cycle of really last-minute chaos. That the people it’s hurting are the voters themselves and the election administrators who are nonpartisan actors usually, and are just trying to get the ballots out. And I also don’t think it’s gonna stop. I would keep an eye on this theme going into 2028. Harris: To that point, the president is highly supportive of redistricting, right? And as you mentioned, Maddie, you wouldn’t expect some of these races to be as close as they are, given that they were redrawn for these specific purposes. Last week, the Cook Political Report moved fifteen races over towards Democrats, saying that they could pick up somewhere between five and fifteen seats there. There are of course valid reasons to redraw district maps. But in an election year, could this not also be seen as a form of cheating, in its own way? With all of the talk of election interference and foreign interference, could this not be seen as a form of domestic interference in our own elections? Carlisle: I think a lot of voters do feel that way. So on the Missouri example I was talking about, Kansas City has been represented for years and years and years by Democrat Emmanuel Cleaver. And then, under the map that was drawn and passed by the Republican legislature, that city—what was done to it is the term “cracking,” in the study of gerrymandering, the term is called cracking. And so basically, I found a church that I think really exemplifies this process. So it used to be and still is a center of the community in northeast Kansas City, this church. But under the map that was drawn by the Republican legislature, the church building itself would be in one district, the parking lot would be another district, and across the street, at the market that they go to, would be a third district. And so that shows this cracking effect, which is when a historically blue or historically red—whatever sort of area the gerrymandering is targeting—is drawn up into these other areas, and to dilute, in a way, the voting power of those areas. And people in Missouri that I was talking to very much felt that way—that they were being disenfranchised by this. Kansas City, arguably, is a cohesive community that had a single Democratic representative for many, many years. And then now these folks that I was talking to, who attend this church, were going to be in a district that was shared with rural Missourian farmers, who have very little of the same interests in, and don’t share a lot of the same concerns that one would bring to a lawmaker. And so that’s all to say, the people I was talking to in Missouri really did feel like their vote was being diluted. It added to the sense that, Why should I cast my ballot? It doesn’t matter; it’s all rigged anyway. These are things that I was hearing from people given the chaos over the drawing of maps in Missouri. I think whether or not it actually is something that is disenfranchising, the Supreme Court has very much proved it in recent Supreme Court decisions. I don’t think it’s going away. And the validity of it as a political tool is something that is certainly being endorsed at this moment by both parties. But the voters, themselves, I do think are feeling that they are losing their ability to further engage in the electoral process because of this fear that, Where I live, will that just be carved up more? So I don’t have an answer for you, but certainly people feel the way you’re describing. Harris: I’m gonna ask both of you to open your notebooks. We’re a little under forty days until the election. What are some of the things that you will be thinking about as we get closer to election day? Tolu, I’ll start with you. Olorunnipa: I’ll be really interested to see how much the bottom falls out of the president’s political standing and of his allies as they approach November. And when I say that, I mean we have heard and seen that some pollsters and some strategists on the Republican side have said that people who won their races by 15 points now should be considered as toss-ups. And that gets you pretty far and pretty deep into people that have shown full support for President Trump, who have felt that they have no concern that once they win their primary, they’re a shoo-in for winning their re-elections. If we start to see some of those folks start to panic even more, and start to distance themselves from the president even more, I think that’ll be a good sense for how much the bottom is falling out and what that means for not only the next forty-odd days, but as we enter into this new phase of President Trump becoming a lame duck. Having no more elections that he can really influence in from the position of power, other than trying to determine his successor, what does that transition look like? What does he do differently, especially if he loses the House and or the Senate, and his power is diminished? How does that change his presidency? How does that change his outlook on power? How much does that change the way he tries to shape his last two years in office? And I think we’ll start seeing it pretty soon after November. Harris: Maddie, same question to you. Carlisle: I am very interested to see how the relationship with the federal government and the states over election administration changes after the November election. I think there has been a lot of concern that the antagonistic relationship the federal government has taken with states when it comes to how they should run their elections, how they should keep their voter rolls. There’s been a lot of concern about how that could change after the election. Is the federal government going to challenge some results? Or is a local candidate going to challenge a result? And is the federal government going to come in and support that candidate? And so I will be watching very closely to see how that relationship between the Justice Department and various states changes, because that’s been something people have been very concerned about. The federal government has not gotten the changes to election administration it broadly wanted. The Supreme Court struck down the changes to mail-in ballots that the president wanted. To Tolu’s point, the save system that they have been seeking to use—DHS’s save system—to purge voter rolls or check voter rolls, the Supreme Court said in its opinion they can’t do that in this 90-day period. But I’d be very interested to see if maybe that system is invoked if some election results are challenged, like Tolu said. So I think it’s definitely going to be important to watch what happens coming out of those federal offices once the ballots are in, because up until now, everyone’s just been speculating. We have no idea what’s going to happen. And the courts have been weighing in, but that’s been it. And so I’m very interested to see actually how those actors behave—those federal and state actors behave—once we know who won. Harris: Yeah, absolutely. Well, there is a ton to keep our eyes on and we will be following you all’s reporting as we move closer to election day. Thank you so much for joining and sharing your reporting. Carlisle: Thanks for having me. Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

items.title: Guinée: Sidya Touré exilé jusqu’à la tombe, quête sans fin de justice après le 28 Septembre!
items.description: Ainsi donc, Sidya Touré, 81 ans, décédé le Z5 septembre 2026 à l’hôpital américain de Neuilly en France, ne sera pas inhumé en Guinée, mais bien en terre ivoirienne, son pays d’exil de son vivant. A moins d’une décision contraire de dernière minute, il en sera ainsi et les obsèques seront, financièrement, prises en charge par le président ivoirien, Alassane Ouattara. Comment en est-on arrivé là? Ce sont nos confrères guinéens qui ont sorti le son. «Malgré le souhait des autorités guinéennes, qui avaient dépêché l’ambassadeur de Guinée en Côte d’Ivoire au domicile du défunt, la famille a choisi Abidjan pour les obsèques. Les enfants évoquent notamment l’absence de domicile familial à Conakry, la maison familiale ayant été reprise par le pouvoir en place.» Autant c’est presque logique que Alassane Ouattara, qui a donné gîte et couvert à son ancien collaborateur, lorsque celui-ci a fui son pays, injecte de l’argent dans ses funérailles, autant c’est incompréhensible et presqu’ahurissant que le défunt, ancien Premier ministre et infatigable serviteur de l’Etat, n’ait pas de «domicile familial» pour accueillir sa dépouille! Le repos éternel sera-t-il possible pour l’illustre disparu, alors que son âme est en errance, loin de la terre de ses ancêtres? Toujours selon nos confrères guinéens, le corps de Sidya Touré serait attendu à Abidjan le 1er octobre, et son inhumation programmée pour le lendemain. Une mort au bout d’un si long exil qui vient confirmer, la situation d’extrême précarité des droits de l’homme dans une Guinée qui a célébré, ce 28 septembre, le douloureux et triste anniversaire du massacre du 28 septembre 2009 dont le bilan macabre affiche au moins 156 morts, des centaines de femmes violées à ciel ouvert et des milliers de blessés. Et les victimes et familles de victimes attendent toujours réparation, suite au procès historique, et fleuve, qui a été organisé 15 ans après le drame. Pendant ce temps, le pouvoir du général Mamady Doumbouya installe une véritable chape de plomb sur le pays. Les grains s’ajoutent au long chapelet des maux dont souffrent des populations qui ne savent plus à quel saint se vouer. Les arrestations arbitraires se multiplient se multiplient, tout comme les disparitions inexpliquées de politiques et de militants de la société civile, la dissolution de partis de l’opposition, les suspension et fermeture de médias nationaux et internationaux, la contrainte de leaders politiques à l’exil, et bien d’autres violations des droits humains. Des dérives qui maintiennent la Guinée dans une quête de justice sans fin. Pourtant, le coup d’Etat de Mamady Doumbouya, le 5 septembre 2021, avait été applaudi à tout rompre par un peuple qui se croyait libéré du régime de fer du Professeur Alpha Condé, l’ancien opposant devenu président et qui, finalement, s’est laissé séduire par les charmes du 3e mandat! Depuis lors, la Guinée semble aller de Charybde en Scylla, avec un pouvoir qui s’est offert une virginité par les urnes, à travers des élections qui ressemblent à toutes celles organisées en Afrique, où la victoire est toujours volée aux challengers battant pavillon opposition, quand il y en a! Ainsi va la Guinée du général Mamady Doumbouya, celui-là même qui n’accepte les opposants que lorsque ceux-ci sont loin de Conakry! Exemples: l’ancien président de la république Alpha Condé et les anciens Premiers ministres, Cellou Dalein Diallo et Sidya Touré! Par Wakat Séra L’article Guinée: Sidya Touré exilé jusqu’à la tombe, quête sans fin de justice après le 28 Septembre! est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
